The Orevkov invariant of an affine plane curve

Walter D. Neumann Address: Department of Mathematics
Columbia University
NY 10027
USA Email address: neumann@math.columbia.edu and Paul Norbury Address: Department of Pure Mathematics
Adelaide University
Australia 5005 Email address: pnorbury@maths.adelaide.edu.au
Abstract.

We show that although the fundamental group of the complement of an algebraic affine plane curve is not easy to compute, it possesses a more accessible quotient, which we call the Orevkov invariant.

1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
14H30, 14R10, 57M25

1. Introduction.

An interesting topological invariant of an algebraic affine plane curve Σ⊂ℂ2\Sigma\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{2} is its link at infinity LΣL_{\Sigma} obtained by intersecting Σ\Sigma with a large sphere in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}. It is quite easily computed using [9, 10].

From LΣL_{\Sigma} and the number of reducible components of Σ\Sigma one can retrieve the arithmetic genus of Σ\Sigma [9, 10], and much about the topology of the defining polynomial ff given by Σ={f=0}\Sigma=\{f=0\} including the topology of its generic fibre and information about its local and global monodromy representations [4, 11]. The link LΣL_{\Sigma} also enables one to obtain geometric information about the curve beyond homological information [12]. This raises the question: how much can LΣL_{\Sigma} tell us about π1​(ℂ2−Σ)\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma)?

If Σ\Sigma is a generic fibre of its defining polynomial ff then LΣL_{\Sigma} gives the topology of Σ\Sigma as an embedded curve in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} and hence it determines π1​(ℂ2−Σ)\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma) (in fact, π1​(ℂ2−Σ)=ℤ\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma)={\mathbb{Z}} in this case by Oka [15]. See Section 2, Theorem 2.2.) In contrast, the cuspidal and nodal curves x2=y3x^{2}=y^{3} and x2=y3+1x^{2}=y^{3}+1 both have the trefoil at infinity whereas the fundamental groups of their complements are respectively the braid group {a,b|aba=bab}\{a,b|aba=bab\} and ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. This leads us to consider a common quotient of the different fundamental groups.

Definition 1.

If pp is a singular point of a plane curve Σ\Sigma, let Gp=π1​(Bp∩(ℂ2−Σ))G_{p}=\pi_{1}(B_{p}\cap({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma)) for a sufficiently small ball BpB_{p} around pp. The Orevkov invariant of Σ\Sigma is

𝒪⁡(Σ)=G/N{\mathcal{O}}(\Sigma)=G/N

where G=π1​(ℂ2−Σ)G=\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma) and NN is the normal closure in GG of the union over all singular points pp of Σ\Sigma of the images of the commutator subgroups [Gp,Gp][G_{p},G_{p}].

Remark. The image of GpG_{p} in GG is only well-defined up to conjugation but since we take the normal closure, NN is well-defined.

When the invariant 𝒪⁡(Σ){\mathcal{O}}(\Sigma) is abelian it is H1​(ℂ2−Σ)=ℤkH_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma)={\mathbb{Z}}^{k}, where kk is the number of irreducible components of Σ\Sigma. This invariant was first studied by Orevkov in [17] who proved that it is abelian when LΣL_{\Sigma} is a positive braid. (He also showed that the invariant is abelian on projective plane curves which generalises the (solved) Zariski conjecture [16].) The invariant ignores the complications of configurations of hyperplanes since it is abelian in these cases.

In this paper we will show that the Orevkov invariant of an algebraic affine plane curve is invariant under a special class of deformations of the curve. By “deformation” we would normally mean a complex analytic family, but the deformations we consider need only be complex analytic near the singularities.

Definition 2.

A deformation of a singularity germ is local component preserving (LCP) if it does not change the number of local irreducible components near the singularity. An LCP deformation of a curve is a deformation that is an LCP deformation in a neighbourhood of each singularity, and is a smooth proper isotopy outside smaller neighbourhoods of the singularities.

This definition applies to projective or affine curves. For affine curves the condition that the isotopy is proper means that the link at infinity is preserved. For example, if Σ\Sigma is the image of a non-constant analytic map f0:ℂ→ℂ2f_{0}\colon{\mathbb{C}}\to{\mathbb{C}}^{2} then any complex analytic deformation ftf_{t} of f0f_{0} which preserves the link at infinity gives an LCP deformation of Σ\Sigma. Examples of non-LCP deformations are:

  1. (1)

    the deformation Σϵ={(x,y):x​y=ϵ}\Sigma_{\epsilon}=\{(x,y):xy=\epsilon\} of Σ0={(x,y):x​y=0}\Sigma_{0}=\{(x,y):xy=0\} (not LCP at the singularity);

  2. (2)

    the deformation Σϵ={(x,y):x​y2+y=ϵ}\Sigma_{\epsilon}=\{(x,y):xy^{2}+y=\epsilon\} of Σ0={(x,y):x​y2+y=0}\Sigma_{0}=\{(x,y):xy^{2}+y=0\} (not proper; link at infinity is not preserved).

Theorem 1.

The Orevkov invariant is invariant under LCP deformations.

A polynomially parametrised curve is a curve with irreducible components given by algebraic maps from ℂ{\mathbb{C}} to ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}. Each irreducible component can be parametrised by a pair of single variable polynomials and is thus a rational curve with one place at infinity.

Polynomially parametrised curves arise naturally as the set of non-generic regular values of a self-map of ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} as follows. Consider a polynomial map F:ℂ2→ℂ2F:{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}^{2} with two-dimensional image. The pre-image of a generic value consists of dd points, say. There are two classes of non-generic values: those that are regular and those that are irregular. The pre-image of a non-generic regular value consists of fewer than dd points. The closure (in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}) of the set of non-generic regular values is a polynomially parametrised curve. This is because the missing points in the pre-image lie “at infinity”. If we compactify ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} by including a divisor at infinity so that F¯\bar{F} is well-defined there, then the points of the divisor at infinity that map to finite values under F¯\bar{F} consist of some of the rational curves of the divisor at infinity. These rational curves are disjoint and each ratonal curve consists of exactly one point that is mapped to infinity, and hence the image of the union of the ratonal curves is a polynomially parametrised curve. The image of the rational curves at infinity might intersect the set of irregular values and hence it gives the closure (in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}) of the non-generic regular points.

If one restricts to deformations of a polynomially parametrised curve that remain within the class of polynomially parametrised curves, then automatically the LCP condition is satisfied at singularities. Hence, from Theorem 1, we see that in many cases the Orevkov invariant of a polynomially parametrised curve is related to its link at infinity.

Corollary 1.1.

The Orevkov invariant of a polynomially parametrised curve depends only on its link at infinity when the moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves with that link at infinity is connected.

Let XΣX_{\Sigma} be a compactification of ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} on which Σ\Sigma meets the divisor at infinity DD transversally. The link at infinity LΣL_{\Sigma} encodes the minimal such divisor DD (see, e.g., [10]) and it also encodes the canonical class of XΣX_{\Sigma} supported on DD. Each component of the link corresponds to a rational curve in DD, known as a horizontal curve. When the canonical class at each link component is negative enough on each horizontal curve we can prove that the moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves with link at infinity LΣL_{\Sigma} is connected and use this to prove the following theorem.

Theorem 2.

For sufficiently negative canonical class on each horizontal curve of XΣX_{\Sigma}, the Orevkov invariant 𝒪⁡(Σ){\mathcal{O}}(\Sigma) of a polynomially parametrised curve Σ\Sigma is abelian.

We state precisely how negative is sufficient in Section 5.2, Theorem 5.2, and in Section 5.3 we show that the class of positive braids LΣL_{\Sigma} is strictly contained in this set. Note that Orevkov [17] proved that the Orevkov invariant is abelian on any curve with positive braid at infinity, not just polynomially parametrised curves with such a property. Since our sufficiently negative condition is only a mild improvement of Orevkov’s result in the polynomially parametrised case, it is the connectivity of certain moduli spaces proved in this paper that is the more significant improvement of his result.

An example of a link at infinity that satisfies the conditions of Theorem 2 is the (5,2)(5,2) cabling on the (2,3)(2,3) torus knot, which is not a positive braid, and represented by the following splice diagram:

2. Nodal curves.

When the curve Σ\Sigma is a nodal curve—its only singularities are simple double points—then 𝒪⁡(Σ)=π1​(ℂ2−Σ){\mathcal{O}}(\Sigma)=\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma). The fundamental group of the complement of a nodal plane curve has a long history beginning with the Zariski conjecture, proven by Deligne [3] and Fulton [6], that the complement of a projective plane nodal curve has abelian fundamental group. This was generalised by Nori [14] to projective and affine curves in smooth surfaces.

Theorem 2.1 (Nori).

Let Σ\Sigma and DD be curves on a smooth projective surface XX, that intersect transversally. Assume that Σ\Sigma is nodal. Denote the number of singular points on a curve CC by r⁡(C)r(C). Assume that C⋅C>2​r​(C)C\cdot C>2r(C) for every irreducible component CC of Σ\Sigma. Then, if NN denotes the kernel of π1​(X−Σ∪D)→π1​(X−D)\pi_{1}(X-\Sigma\cup D)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(X-D), NN is a finitely generated abelian group and the centraliser of NN is a subgroup of finite index.

In particular, when Σ\Sigma is a nodal curve in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}, and XX the blow-up of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} that resolves the singularities of Σ\Sigma at infinity, and D=X−ℂ2D=X-{\mathbb{C}}^{2} the divisor at infinity, if Σ¯i⋅Σ¯i>2​r​(Σi)\bar{\Sigma}_{i}\cdot\bar{\Sigma}_{i}>2r(\Sigma_{i}) for each irreducible component Σi\Sigma_{i} of Σ\Sigma then π1​(ℂ2−Σ)\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma) is abelian (since X−D=ℂ2X-D={\mathbb{C}}^{2} and N=π1​(ℂ2−Σ)N=\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma) in the theorem.)

As mentioned in the introduction, when Σ\Sigma is the generic fibre of its defining polynomial, LΣL_{\Sigma} determines π1​(ℂ2−Σ)\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma).

Theorem 2.2 (Oka [15]).

If Σ\Sigma is the generic fibre of a polynomial ff then π1​(ℂ2−Σ)=ℤ\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma)={\mathbb{Z}}.

Proof.

Choose a disk Ds⊂ℂD_{s}\subset{\mathbb{C}} to contain all of the atypical values of ff and a small disjoint disk DcD_{c} that gives a neighbourhood of c=f⁡(Σ)c=f(\Sigma). Join the disks by a path γ\gamma and put D′=Ds∪γ∪DcD^{\prime}=D_{s}\cup\gamma\cup D_{c}. Then each of the following arrows is a homotopy equivalence:

f−1​(Ds)↪f−1​(Ds∪γ)↪f−1​(D′)↪ℂ2f^{-1}(D_{s})\hookrightarrow f^{-1}(D_{s}\cup\gamma)\hookrightarrow f^{-1}(D^{\prime})\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{C}}^{2}
f−1​(D′−{c})↪ℂ2−Σ.f^{-1}(D^{\prime}-\{c\})\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma.

Apply the Seifert Van-Kampen theorem to

f−1​(D′−{c})=f−1​(Ds∪γ)∪f−1​(Dc−{c}).f^{-1}(D^{\prime}-\{c\})=f^{-1}(D_{s}\cup\gamma)\cup f^{-1}(D_{c}-\{c\}).

Since f−1​(Dc−{c})≅(Dc−{c})×Σ∼S1×Σf^{-1}(D_{c}-\{c\})\cong(D_{c}-\{c\})\times\Sigma\sim S^{1}\times\Sigma we get that π1​(ℂ2−Σ)\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma) is the quotient of π1​(ℂ2)∗π1​(S1×Σ)=π1​(S1×Σ)\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2})*\pi_{1}(S^{1}\times\Sigma)=\pi_{1}(S^{1}\times\Sigma) by the normal closure of π1​(Σ)\pi_{1}(\Sigma), and thus π1​(ℂ2−Σ)=ℤ\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma)={\mathbb{Z}}. ∎

Remark. It is amusing to note that Theorem 2.2 is almost a consequence of Theorem 2.1 which requires Σ¯⋅Σ¯>0=2​r​(Σ)\bar{\Sigma}\cdot\bar{\Sigma}>0=2r(\Sigma) to conclude that π1​(ℂ2−Σ)\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma) is abelian. The self-intersection number of the generic fibre of a polynomial is non-negative. It is given as a sum over linking numbers of components of LΣL_{\Sigma}. In [10] it was shown that the polynomial is irregular at a point at infinity precisely when the linking number for the corresponding link component is 00. In particular, for a good polynomial, one which is never irregular at infinity, the self-intersection number of the generic fibre is strictly positive and Theorem 2.1 implies Theorem 2.2. In fact, Theorem 2.1 applies in most cases since it is quite rare that the generic fibre of a polynomial has zero self-intersection, or equivalently that it is irregular at infinity at each link component of LΣL_{\Sigma}. Russell’s bad field generator [18] and each polynomial in Kaliman’s classification of rational polynomials with a ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*} fibre [7] are examples of polynomials whose generic fibre has zero self-intersection number, and hence Theorem 2.1 does not imply Theorem 2.2 in these cases.

This paper will consist mainly of examples of curves with abelian Orevkov invariant. Two examples with non-abelian invariant are as follows.

(i) For f:ℂ2→ℂf:{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}} the curve Σ=f−1​(A)\Sigma=f^{-1}(A) for a finite set of at least two points A⊂ℂA\subset{\mathbb{C}} has non-abelian Orevkov invariant.

(ii) The following example was constructed by Mutsuo Oka. Let

f⁡(x,y)=(x2−y)2​y−4​x​(x2−y)+4=0.f(x,y)=(x^{2}-y)^{2}y-4x(x^{2}-y)+4=0.

Then Σ=f−1​(0)\Sigma=f^{-1}(0) is a smooth irreducible curve with

π1(ℂ2−Σ)={a,b|aba=bab}=𝒪(Σ).\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma)=\{a,b|aba=bab\}={\mathcal{O}}(\Sigma).

3. Invariance under local deformations.

In this section we will prove Theorem 1 by showing that it reduces easily to an argument of Orevkov’s.

Proof.

Given a plane curve Σ\Sigma, we can enclose its singularities in small balls BiB_{i} and compute π1​(ℂ2−Σ)\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma) by the Van Kampen theorem in terms of the fundamental groups of the complement of Σ\Sigma in each of the balls as well as their exterior X=ℂ2−⋃iBiX={\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\bigcup_{i}B_{i}. Under an LCP deformation, we can assume that the topology of X−(Σ∩X)X-(\Sigma\cap X) does not change, so it suffices to show that the Orevkov invariant of each (Bi,Bi∩Σ)(B_{i},B_{i}\cap\Sigma) also does not change.

We therefore restrict to the local situation, in which we have a germ of a singularity (Σ,p)(\Sigma,p) and a small ball BB around pp such that its boundary and the boundary of all smaller balls centered at pp intersect Σ\Sigma transversally. We take a LCP deformation that changes the intersection of Σ\Sigma with ∂B\partial B only by an isotopy. In this situation we must show that the Orevkov invariant of (B,B∩Σ)(B,B\cap\Sigma) does not change. We may change coordinates so that pp is the origin and Σ\Sigma is given by an equation f⁡(x,y)=0f(x,y)=0 of degree nn with f⁡(x,y)=xn+an−1​(y)​xn−1+⋯+a0​(y)f(x,y)=x^{n}+a_{n-1}(y)x^{n-1}+\dots+a_{0}(y). We may then take the ball BB to be polydisk {(x,y):|x|≤ϵ1,|y|≤ϵ2}=D1×D2\{(x,y):|x|\leq\epsilon_{1},|y|\leq\epsilon_{2}\}=D_{1}\times D_{2}, chosen such that Σ\Sigma intersects ∂B\partial B only in the portion ∂D1×D2\partial D_{1}\times D_{2}. Finally, we may assume our coordinates are chosen so that the set of xx for which Σ∩B\Sigma\cap B contains more than one point (x,y)(x,y) whose yy-coordinates have the same real part is in generic position in the sense of Orevkov’s papers [16] and [17], both before and after our deformation. We denote this set

P:={x∈D1:∃y1≠y2 with (x,y1)∈Σ,(x,y2)∈Σ,ℜy1=ℜy2}.P:=\{x\in D_{1}:\exists~y_{1}\neq y_{2}\text{ with }(x,y_{1})\in\Sigma,(x,y_{2})\in\Sigma,\Re y_{1}=\Re y_{2}\}.

Generic position implies that PP consists of a collection of paths oriented by increasing |y1−y2||y_{1}-y_{2}|. Before deforming Σ\Sigma, these paths start at the image of the one singular point and fan out to ∂D1\partial D_{1}, since we choose the ball small enough that the only singular point of the projection B∩Σ→D1B\cap\Sigma\to D_{1} is the singular point of Σ\Sigma. After the deformation there may be several singular points, but we may assume that the behavior of the paths near ∂D1\partial D_{1} has changed only by an isotopy. The paths then still start at singular values of the projection B∩Σ→D1B\cap\Sigma\to D_{1} and end at the boundary of the disk. Moreover, away from singular points of the projection B∩Σ→D1B\cap\Sigma\to D_{1}, the paths may now intersect, but Orevkov’s genericity condition says they intersect at most in pairs or in triples, and these intersections are transverse (the triple intersections arise when three real parts of yy-values coincide at a time). The projection B∩Σ→D1B\cap\Sigma\to D_{1} is a covering map on the inverse image of D1−PD_{1}-P, of degree dd, say, and, as in [16], one can give a presentation of π1​(B−Σ)\pi_{1}(B-\Sigma) with dd generators for each component of D1−PD_{1}-P, and with relations associated to the singular points of B∩Σ→D1B\cap\Sigma\to D_{1} and to the intersection points of paths comprising PP. The same inductive argument that Orevkov uses, moving along the paths starting from the singular points, then shows that the Orevkov invariant is free abelian with one generator for each irreducible component of B∩ΣB\cap\Sigma. ∎

4. Splice diagrams.

A convenient way to represent the link at infinity of an affine plane algebraic curve uses the splice diagram of the link. The splice diagram of a link at infinity can be viewed as a cabled torus knot in S3S^{3}, or the Puiseux expansion of the affine curve at infinity given by expressing one coordinate in terms of the other, or the plumbing graph of an efficient resolution at infinity of the affine curve. We will demonstrate these three views by focusing on the example of a curve with knot at infinity. This includes irreducible polynomial curves. The splice diagram of such a curve is given by

where the pairs of integers (pk,qk)(p_{k},q_{k}) are known as weights of the splice diagram and the CkC_{k} are simply labels for the valency one nodes.

The splice diagram represents a knot obtained by cabling a (p2,q2)(p_{2},q_{2}) torus knot on a (p1,q1)(p_{1},q_{1}) torus knot and then cabling a (p3,q3)(p_{3},q_{3}) torus knot on that, and so on. The earlier torus knots are represented as “virtual” link components in the diagram by the valency one nodes CkC_{k}. For example, the components C0C_{0} and C1C_{1} form a Hopf link and the component C2C_{2} is a (p1,q1)(p_{1},q_{1}) torus knot cabled on C1C_{1}. The arrowhead represents the actual knot, a (pn,qn)(p_{n},q_{n}) cabling on the virtual knot CnC_{n}.

The linking number of any two (virtual) components can be calculated from the splice diagram. It is the product of all weights incident to a path joining the two nodes. Thus, l⁡(Cj,Ck)=pj​qj+1​…​qkl(C_{j},C_{k})=p_{j}q_{j+1}\dots q_{k} and if we denote the knot (represented by the arrowhead) by KK, then l⁡(Ck,K)=pk​qk+1​…​qnl(C_{k},K)=p_{k}q_{k+1}\dots q_{n}.

Not all knots arise as the knot at infinity of a plane curve. Necessary and sufficent conditions on the weights of a splice diagram of a knot at infinity are:

(1) {i.pk>1,qk>1,(pk,qk)=1ii.Δk=pk−pk−1​qk−1​qk<0andΔ1=pk−qk<0iii.pk+1∈ℕ​q1​q2​…​qk⊕ℕ​p1​q2​…​qk⊕⋯⊕ℕ​pk−1​qk⊕ℕ​pk\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}{\rm i}.\ p_{k}>1,\ q_{k}>1,\ (p_{k},q_{k})=1\\ {\rm ii}.\ \Delta_{k}=p_{k}-p_{k-1}q_{k-1}q_{k}<0\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Delta_{1}=p_{k}-q_{k}<0\\ {\rm iii}.\ p_{k+1}\in{\mathbb{N}}q_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{k}\oplus{\mathbb{N}}p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{k}\oplus\dots\oplus{\mathbb{N}}p_{k-1}q_{k}\oplus{\mathbb{N}}p_{k}\end{array}\right.

The third rather deep property involving linking numbers of virtual link components is the semi-group condition of Abhyankar and Moh [1].

The splice diagram also gives an efficient resolution around the point of Σ\Sigma at infinity. Compactify ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} to ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} and let 𝒫⁡(y,z)=0{\mathcal{P}}(y,z)=0 define Σ¯\overline{\Sigma} in a neighbourhood of the point [1:0:0]∈ℙ2[1:0:0]\in{\mathbb{P}}^{2} (which we have supposed to be the point where Σ¯\overline{\Sigma} meets the line at infinity.) Each characteristic pair in the splice diagram encodes a multiple blow-up of the resolution of the point at infinity. To resolve at the kkth step, one replaces (y,z)(y,z) by (ya​z−Δk+Qk​(yb​zqk),yb​zqk)(y^{a}z^{-\Delta_{k}}+Q_{k}(y^{b}z^{q_{k}}),y^{b}z^{q_{k}}) where a,b>0a,b>0 are chosen so that a​qk+b​Δk=1aq_{k}+b\Delta_{k}=1. The single variable polynomial QkQ_{k} is uniquely determined. The curve Σ¯\overline{\Sigma} is “resolved” at infinity when it meets the divisor at infinity transversally. Each node CkC_{k} represents a curve in the divisor at infinity and the defining polynomial of the curve Σ¯\overline{\Sigma} in a neighbourhood of CkC_{k} is the polynomial obtained at the kkth step of the resolution.

The approximate roots of the defining polynomial P⁡(x,y)P(x,y) of Σ\Sigma

Consider all holomorphic functions on Σ\Sigma, meromorphic at infinity. The orders of the poles of these functions form a semi-group in ℕ{\mathbb{N}} known as the Weierstrass semi-group, with complement the Weierstrass gap sequence. Using Riemann-Roch, the size of the Weierstrass gap sequence can be shown to be equal to the arithmetic genus gg of Σ\Sigma which is easily calculated in terms of the splice diagram:

5. Polynomially parametrised curves.

If Σ\Sigma is a polynomially parametrised curve then any deformation within the class of polynomially parametrised curves preserves the irreducible components globally and hence locally. Hence any such deformation that also preserves the link at infinity is an LCP deformation and we can apply Theorem 1 to show that the Orevkov invariant of Σ\Sigma depends only upon its connected component of polynomially parametrised curves with a given link at infinity.

In this section we will describe the moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves. This will allow us to study the connected components of the moduli space and in particular when such moduli spaces are connected.

5.1. Moduli spaces.

We will begin with a description of the moduli space of irreducible polynomially parametrised curves with a given splice diagram at infinity.

Theorem 5.1.

Let the pair of polynomials (x⁡(t),y⁡(t))(x(t),y(t)) define a reduced rational curve Σ\Sigma. Then the following two properties are equivalent:

(A) the link at infinity of Σ\Sigma has splice diagram

(B) The defining polynomial for Σ\Sigma is given by P(x,y)=yn+1(x,y1,y2,..,yn)P(x,y)=y_{n+1}(x,y_{1},y_{2},..,y_{n}) where y1=yy_{1}=y and for each k=1,…,nk=1,...,n,

(4) yk+1(x,y1,y2,..,yk)=ykqk+∑eaexe0y1e1y2e2..ykeky_{k+1}(x,y_{1},y_{2},..,y_{k})=y_{k}^{q_{k}}+\sum_{e}a_{e}x^{e_{0}}y_{1}^{e_{1}}y_{2}^{e_{2}}..y_{k}^{e_{k}}

where e=(e0,..,ek)e=(e_{0},..,e_{k}) is summed over all tuples such that the order of the pole at ∞\infty (the tt-degree) of the corresponding monomial is no greater than the order of the pole at ∞\infty of ykqky_{k}^{q_{k}}. As a polynomial in tt, degt⁡yk=pk​qk+1​qk+2​…​qn\deg_{t}y_{k}=p_{k}q_{k+1}q_{k+2}\dots q_{n} for (pk,qk)=1(p_{k},q_{k})=1 and yn+1≡0y_{n+1}\equiv 0.

Proof.

Given a curve parametrised by (x⁡(t),y⁡(t))(x(t),y(t)), there is an algorithm to determine the polynomial which vanishes on the curve, P⁡(x,y)=0P(x,y)=0. The splice diagram at infinity guides the algorithm and the holomorphic functions {y2,…,yn}\{y_{2},\dots,y_{n}\} with the stated properties are produced along the way. The algorithm runs as follows.

Take a linear combination y10=yq1+λ​xp1y_{10}=y^{q_{1}}+\lambda x^{p_{1}} so that d​e​gt​y10<p1​q1deg_{t}y_{10}<p_{1}q_{1}. This procedure stops when we can no longer reduce the degree using monomials in xx and yy and produces y2​(x,y)y_{2}(x,y) with pole at infinity of order degt⁡y2=p2​q3​…​qn\deg_{t}y_{2}=p_{2}q_{3}\dots q_{n} for the following reason.

For x⁡(t)=∑ai​tix(t)=\sum a_{i}t^{i} and y=∑bj​tjy=\sum b_{j}t^{j} the variety is given as a set of polynomial equations in the coefficients {ai,bj}\{a_{i},b_{j}\} as follows.

The expression for yk+1y_{k+1} in (4) a priori has tt-degree pk​qk​qk+1..qnp_{k}q_{k}q_{k+1}..q_{n} but since we require that yk+1y_{k+1} has tt-degree pk+1​qk+2​qk+3..qn<pk​qk​qk+1..qnp_{k+1}q_{k+2}q_{k+3}..q_{n}<p_{k}q_{k}q_{k+1}..q_{n}, by (1) ii, then each of the coefficients of tmt^{m} for pk​qk​qk+1..qn≥m>pk+1​qk+2​qk+3..qnp_{k}q_{k}q_{k+1}..q_{n}\geq m>p_{k+1}q_{k+2}q_{k+3}..q_{n} must vanish. For m∈Wkm\in W_{k}, defined in (5), the coefficient of tmt^{m} is canceled by a monomial in xx and yiy_{i}, i≤ki\leq k. For each m∉Wkm\notin W_{k} , define Tm,k​({ai,bj})T_{m,k}(\{a_{i},b_{j}\}) to be the coefficient of tmt^{m} in yky_{k}. We call the variety {Tm,k=0}\{T_{m,k}=0\} the moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves with given splice diagram at infinity.

Each polynomial Tm,kT_{m,k} has the property that it only depends on bjb_{j} and aia_{i} for i≥e⁡(k)−mi\geq e(k)-m, where e⁡(1)=p1​q1​q2​…​qne(1)=p_{1}q_{1}q_{2}\ldots q_{n} and e⁡(k)=e⁡(k−1)+(qk−1)​pk​qk+1​…​qne(k)=e(k-1)+(q_{k}-1)p_{k}q_{k+1}\ldots q_{n}, and if equality occurs then that coefficient appears in Tm,kT_{m,k} linearly with non-zero coefficient. By non-zero coefficient, we mean that it is a polynomial in the {bj}\{b_{j}\} that is required to be non-zero (earlier in the algorithm.)

When the link at infinity has more than one component, or equivalently the polynomially parametrised curves are reducible, if the splice components meet only on the root vertex, or equivalently the curve components do not intersect at infinity, then the moduli space is simply a product of the moduli spaces for each component, minus a divisor along which the curves meet at infinity. In general, any two irreducible components of the link at infinity agree along an initial iterated cabling and this introduces a further equation giving equality of the initial coefficients of the respective pairs of polynomials.

It is often difficult to tell when the variety is connected or even when it is non-empty. In the case of a knot at infinity, the semi-group theorem of Abhyankar and Moh [1] and its converse by Sathaye and Stenerson [19] give necessary and sufficient conditions for the moduli space of curves (not necessarily rational) to be non-empty.

5.2. Solving the equations.

In the previous section we constructed a variety that gives the moduli space of an irreducible component of a polynomially parametrised curve with a given link at infinity. In this section we will be more explicit, and solve the equations for a given link at infinity. It is important to note that we only consider splice diagrams that are links at infinity of algebraic curves so Δk=pk−pk−1​qk−1​qk<0\Delta_{k}=p_{k}-p_{k-1}q_{k-1}q_{k}<0 for all kk.

We will begin with a short discussion of the canonical class divisor associated to LΣL_{\Sigma}. The splice diagram for LΣL_{\Sigma} gives an efficient resolution at infinity for Σ\Sigma. It gives the valency >2>2 curves in the plumbing diagram of the divisor at infinity D⊂XΣD\subset X_{\Sigma}. It can be arranged that the canonical class KK of XΣX_{\Sigma} is supported on the divisor DD, so KK is given by a sequence of multiplicities, one for each irreducible curve in DD. At each component of LΣL_{\Sigma}, the multiplicity of KK is given by the local intersection K⋅ΣK\cdot\Sigma at that component. Instead of working with K⋅ΣK\cdot\Sigma, we prefer to work with −K⋅Σ−1-K\cdot\Sigma-1 which we denote by dd at each component of the link, and more generally at each virtual component of the link, or node of the splice diagram.

The number dd can be calculated at a node in the splice diagram of LΣL_{\Sigma} by taking a path from the node to the root—the node that represents the proper transform of ℙ1=ℙ2−ℂ2{\mathbb{P}}^{1}={\mathbb{P}}^{2}-{\mathbb{C}}^{2}—of the splice diagram. Such a path is represented by Figure 2 where other arrows may exist in the diagram at the places marked with dots. If we notate dd at the kkth node by dkd_{k} then dkd_{k} is calculated recursively by

(7) dk=qk​dk−1+Δk,d1=p1+q1.d_{k}=q_{k}d_{k-1}+\Delta_{k},\ \ d_{1}=p_{1}+q_{1}.

The following theorem is a more precise statement of the sufficiently negative condition of Theorem 2.

Theorem 5.2.

When dn≥p1​q2​…​qn−1d_{n}\geq p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n}-1 for each component of LL then the moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves Σ\Sigma with LΣ=LL_{\Sigma}=L is connected.

Proof.

A straight-forward way to solve the equations is to arbitrarily choose the coefficients of y⁡(t)y(t), and solve for the coefficients of x⁡(t)x(t), and use this to show that when the moduli space is non-empty it is connected. As described in the properties of the Tm,kT_{m,k}, the equations Tm,k=0T_{m,k}=0 form a diagonal system in which each coefficient of xx appears for the first time linearly with non-zero coefficient.

For each k=2,…,nk=2,\dots,n, the equation degt⁡yk=pk​qk+1​qk+2​…​qn\deg_{t}y_{k}=p_{k}q_{k+1}q_{k+2}\dots q_{n} gives rise to

(In fact, many coefficients of xx are wasted since we need only solve Tm,k=0T_{m,k}=0 for m∉Wkm\notin W_{k}.) We need:

If, by good fortune, we do get equality each time, then we can calculate the dimension of the space of solutions to the system as the degree of y⁡(t)y(t) plus the number of coefficients of x⁡(t)x(t) unused when solving the system.

Lemma 5.3.

The moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves with given link at infinity is either of the expected dimension and connected, or empty.

Proof.

We have arranged that the coefficient of tpk​qk+1​qk+2​…​qn+1t^{p_{k}q_{k+1}q_{k+2}\dots q_{n}+1} vanishes. The coefficient of tpk​qk+1​qk+2​…​qnt^{p_{k}q_{k+1}q_{k+2}\dots q_{n}} is a polynomial BkB_{k} in the coefficients of y⁡(t)y(t). One of two cases must occur. Either:

(i) the polynomial BkB_{k} is identically zero thus the moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves with that particular link at infinity is empty; or

(ii) the polynomial BkB_{k} is not identically zero thus the coefficients of y⁡(t)y(t) that give a smaller degree for yky_{k} form a set of codimension ≥1\geq 1 and the moduli space of coefficients of y⁡(t)y(t) that give the right degree for yky_{k} is a non-empty connected space. ∎

If each component of LΣL_{\Sigma} gives rise to a non-empty moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves, then by construction we can fit the moduli spaces of the components of Σ\Sigma together to get the full moduli space. Two link components agree along an initial path of cablings, or equivalently the respective compactification divisors at infinity agree on an initial path of blow-ups, when the same top coefficients of y⁡(t)y(t) are chosen along with the same polynomials yky_{k}. Again, accidental agreement along a further path of cablings occurs either on a codimension ≥1\geq 1 set or the moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves with given link at infinity is empty.

This completes the proof of the theorem. ∎

Remarks (i) We can ensure that each non-empty moduli space contains an immersion. When an unused coefficient aia_{i} of xx appears for the first time, and hence linearly, in Tm,kT_{m,k}, say, we can use aia_{i} as a parameter. The polynomial x⁡(t)x(t) then depends on the parameter aia_{i} and (x′​(t),y′​(t))≠(0,0)(x^{\prime}(t),y^{\prime}(t))\neq(0,0) for generic choice of aia_{i}.

(ii) In the next section we prove that for positive braids Lemma 5.3 can be strengthened to show that the space of solutions is always non-empty.

We are now almost in a position to prove Theorem 2. The following lemma proves that a particular class of immersions has abelian fundamental group and hence abelian Orevkov invariant.

5.3. Positive braids.

The link at infinity of an affine algebraic curve inherits a natural braid structure. In fact there is a braid structure for each line in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} obtained by projection along the line. The condition that the splice diagram of a link at infinity gives a positive braid is a condition on the weights pi,qip_{i},q_{i} of each branch of the splice diagram given in Figure 2.

In order to make the largest possible set of links at infinity positive braids, we choose to project along the xx direction (assume degree x⁡(t)>x(t)> degree y⁡(t)y(t)). In the following proposition, if we were to use the braid structure from the projection along the yy direction, then the condition dn>p1​q2​…​qnd_{n}>p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n} would be replaced by dn>q1​q2​…​qn>p1​q2​…​qnd_{n}>q_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n}>p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n} which is a stronger condition and hence fewer links would be positive braids.

Proposition 5.5.

The link at infinity of an affine curve is a positive braid precisely when dn>p1​q2​…​qnd_{n}>p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n} along each path of the splice diagram shown in Figure 2.

Proof.

Each component of a positive braid is again a positive braid so we will restrict to each path in the splice diagram. We will actually prove that dk>p1​q2​…​qkd_{k}>p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{k}, k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n. Thus we claim that the corresponding virtual link components are also positive braids.

Lemma 5.6.

Using the framing supplied by the braid projection, the self-linking number of the braid in Figure 5.3 is

lj=pj​qj+p1​q2​…​qj−dj.l_{j}=p_{j}q_{j}+p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{j}-d_{j}.

Equivalently, it is the braid index of the braid.

Proof.

Prove this by induction. To begin, the (p1,q1)(p_{1},q_{1}) torus knot has self-linking number l1=p1​q1−q1=p1​q1+p1−d1l_{1}=p_{1}q_{1}-q_{1}=p_{1}q_{1}+p_{1}-d_{1}, as required. To see the recursive relationship for ljl_{j}, suppose we cable qj+1q_{j+1} parallel strings along Figure 5.3 using the framing supplied by the braid projection. Then the self-linking number, or braid index, of this new braid is given by qj+12​ljq_{j+1}^{2}l_{j}. Now consider a qj+1q_{j+1} cabling on Figure 5.3 with weight pj+1p_{j+1}. Note that pj+1p_{j+1} gives the linking number of (the virtual copy of) Figure 5.3 with each of the qj+1q_{j+1} cables and a cabling already links qj+1​ljq_{j+1}l_{j} times with (the virtual copy of) Figure 5.3. Thus, the new self-linking number is

(10) lj+1=qj+12​lj+(qj+1−1)​(pj+1−qj+1​lj)=qj+1​lj+qj+1​pj+1−pj+1.l_{j+1}=q_{j+1}^{2}l_{j}+(q_{j+1}-1)(p_{j+1}-q_{j+1}l_{j})=q_{j+1}l_{j}+q_{j+1}p_{j+1}-p_{j+1}.

In particular, lj−pj​qjl_{j}-p_{j}q_{j} and p1​q2​…​qj−djp_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{j}-d_{j} satisfy the same recursion relation. Since l1−p1​q1=p1−d1l_{1}-p_{1}q_{1}=p_{1}-d_{1}, the result follows. ∎

Now, a positive braid arises when the pj+1−qj+1​ljp_{j+1}-q_{j+1}l_{j} extra twists in (10) is positive. Hence pk>lk−1​qkp_{k}>l_{k-1}q_{k}, k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n and dk>p1​q2​…​qkd_{k}>p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{k} for k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n.

Note, too, that the recursive relationship for djd_{j} shows that dn>p1​q2​…​qnd_{n}>p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n} implies dk>p1​q2​…​qkd_{k}>p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{k} for k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n. ∎

Since the condition in Proposition 5.5 is stronger than that in Theorem 5.2 we get the folllowing corollary.

Corollary 5.7.

The moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves with positive braid at infinity is connected.

Proposition 5.8.

The moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves with positive braid at infinity is non-empty.

Proof.

In the proof of Theorem 5.2, we produced points in the variety for a given splice diagram by solving for the coefficients of ff in terms of the coefficients in gg. The variety can be empty when there is accidental vanishing of the coefficients of any of tpk​qk+1..qnt^{p_{k}q_{k+1}..q_{n}} for k=1,..,nk=1,..,n (where nn is the number of Puiseux pairs of the particular component.) Since at each component of a positive braid there are n−1n-1 extra degrees of freedom,

dn≥p1​q2​…​qn+1≥p1​q2​…​qn−1d_{n}\geq p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n}+1\geq p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n}-1

then these can be used to set the coefficients of tpk​qk+1..qnt^{p_{k}q_{k+1}..q_{n}} to be 11. Thus, for each component the moduli space is non-empty.

When we put the components together, components branching off at different points in the splice diagram correspond to different choices of coefficients that lie in the semi-group of the curve, and hence waste no degrees of freedom. Thus the moduli space of polynomial curves with positive braid at infinity is non-empty. ∎

For positive braids, we can prove Theorem 2 without using Nori’s theorem. We used Nori’s theorem to calculate the Orevkov invariant for a special representative in the moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves. For positive braids, we can do such a calculation explicitly.

Theorem 5.9.

Given a curve (F⁡(t),G⁡(t))(F(t),G(t)) define

(f⁡(t),g⁡(t))=(F⁡(td)+ϵ​h​(t),G⁡(td)).(f(t),g(t))=(F(t^{d})+\epsilon h(t),G(t^{d})).

Then for most degree h<dh<d and for small enough ϵ\epsilon the Orevkov invariant of (f⁡(t),g⁡(t))(f(t),g(t)) is a quotient of the Orevkov invariant of (F⁡(t),G⁡(t))(F(t),G(t)).

Proof.

Choose a large ball BRB_{R} that realises the link at infinity of (F⁡(t),G⁡(t))(F(t),G(t)). Choose a path from 00 to ∞\infty in ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*} that avoids self-intersections of (F,G)(F,G). Choose ϵ\epsilon small enough so that a tube of radius ϵ​R\epsilon R intersects the curve (F⁡(td),G⁡(td))(F(t^{d}),G(t^{d})) only in an embedded strip in the curve. Thus along the path the dd deformations remain disjoint from the rest of (F,G)(F,G). The dd deformations may intersect each other. The branch point at t=0t=0 gives the relation that each of the dd elements in the fundamental group are equal. Thus, the Orevkov invariant of the deformed curve (f⁡(t),g⁡(t))=(F⁡(td)+ϵ​t,G⁡(td))(f(t),g(t))=(F(t^{d})+\epsilon t,G(t^{d})) is a quotient of the Orevkov invariant of (F⁡(t),G⁡(t))(F(t),G(t)). The Orevkov invariants are the same if BRB_{R} realises the link at infinity of (f⁡(t),g⁡(t))(f(t),g(t)). ∎

Next we give a construction of a rational curve with positive braid at infinity in order to apply Theorem 5.9.

Theorem 5.10.

If (F⁡(t),G⁡(t))(F(t),G(t)) defines the component of a positive braid

then for degree h⁡(t)<(dn−q1​q2​…​qn)​qn+1h(t)<(d_{n}-q_{1}q_{2}\ldots q_{n})q_{n+1}, the curve

(f⁡(t),g⁡(t))=(F⁡(tqn+1)+ϵ​h​(t),G⁡(tqn+1))(f(t),g(t))=(F(t^{q_{n+1}})+\epsilon h(t),G(t^{q_{n+1}}))

defines the component

where any pn+1p_{n+1} that satisfies pn+1−pn​qn​qn+1+dn​qn+1=dn+1>p1​q2​…​qn​qn+1p_{n+1}-p_{n}q_{n}q_{n+1}+d_{n}q_{n+1}=d_{n+1}>p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n}q_{n+1} is uniquely determined by the choice of hh.

Proof.

When we solve the diagonal system of equations Tm,k=0T_{m,k}=0 for a positive braid at infinity to get (F⁡(t),G⁡(t))(F(t),G(t)), the coefficients of F⁡(t)F(t) appear in order from the highest power of tt to the lowest. Furthermore, the last dn−q1​q2​…​qnd_{n}-q_{1}q_{2}\ldots q_{n} coefficients of F⁡(t)F(t) are irrelevant to the system of equations. If the degree of ϵ​h​(t)\epsilon h(t) is less than (dn−q1​q2​…​qn)​qn+1(d_{n}-q_{1}q_{2}\ldots q_{n})q_{n+1} then ϵ​h​(t)\epsilon h(t) does not affect the equations Tm,k=0T_{m,k}=0 for k<nk<n, and features only in the equations Tm,n=0T_{m,n}=0. The equations Tm,n=0T_{m,n}=0 form a diagonal sustem in the coefficients of ϵ​h​(t)\epsilon h(t) and hence we can solve for any pn+1p_{n+1} that gives rise to a positive braid, or equivalently satsifies the inequality pn+1−pn​qn​qn+1+dn​qn+1=dn+1>p1​q2​…​qn​qn+1p_{n+1}-p_{n}q_{n}q_{n+1}+d_{n}q_{n+1}=d_{n+1}>p_{1}q_{2}\dots q_{n}q_{n+1}. ∎

Thus, by induction the Orevkov invariant of a polynomially parametrised curve Σ\Sigma with positive braid at infinity is abelian since it is a quotient of the Orevkov invariant of a simpler curve obtained by reducing by one the number of Puiseux pairs on a component of Σ\Sigma. Eventually the curve is reduced to a configuration of lines, where the invariant is abelian.

6. Further examples.

The invariance of the Orevkov invariant under LCP deformations reduces the problem of calculating the invariant, or searching for a curve with non-abelian invariant, to understanding the finitely many topological types at infinity of curves with given degree. One can enumerate polynomially parametrised curves by their splice diagrams at infinity and the connected components of the moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves with that splice diagram at infinity. When the curves are irreducible the list for degree up to 1212 is as follows:

In each of the above diagrams, by a,..,ba,..,b we mean all of the odd integers from aa to bb, except in the case of kk in Figure 7, which misses some odd values.

The degree <6<6, 7 and 11 curves have positive braids at infinity and we have not listed them nor positive braids for degree 6, 8, 10 and 12. They are covered by Theorem 2 along with many on the list above (for example, when the degree is 6 only k=3k=3 is not covered.) Using MAPLE for those curves above of degree <12<12 not covered by Theorem 2 we have shown that each moduli space of polynomially parametrised curves is connected and that the Orevkov invariant of each is abelian.

So far we have only been able to calculate the Orevkov invariant of a curve by calculating the fundamental group of the complement of some curve obtained by deforming the original curve and applying Theorem 1. Given the many cases where the Orevkov invariant depends only on the link at infinity we would hope to be able to calculate the invariant without calculating the fundamental group of the complement of a curve.

One can construct smooth examples of curves ℂ→ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}^{2} with non-abelian Orevkov invariant. An example is as follows. Consider the representation of

π1​(ℂ−2​points)={γ1,γ2}\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}-{\rm 2\ points})=\{\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}\}

into the braid group

B3={σ1,σ2|σ1σ2σ1=σ2σ1σ2}B_{3}=\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}|\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\}

given by

γ1↦σ2−2​σ1​σ22andγ2↦σ12​σ2​σ1−2.\gamma_{1}\mapsto\sigma_{2}^{-2}\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}^{2}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\gamma_{2}\mapsto\sigma_{1}^{2}\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1}^{-2}.

This gives rise to a smoothly embedded surface in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} described via two maps from a disk ℂ{\mathbb{C}} to ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. The first map, xx, is a 3-fold branched cover with two branch points. Take a regular point cc for xx and a loop γ\gamma starting and ending at cc that moves around one of the branch points of xx. The pre-image x−1​(γ)x^{-1}(\gamma) is a path containg the three preimages x−1​(c)x^{-1}(c). The second map, yy, is a 2-fold branched cover that wraps x−1​(γ)x^{-1}(\gamma) around its single branch point in such a way that it has a double point.

The map (x,y):ℂ→ℂ2(x,y):{\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}^{2} defines a smoothly embedded surface Σ\Sigma with

π1(ℂ2−Σ)={a,b|aba=bab}.\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}-\Sigma)=\{a,b|aba=bab\}.

This cannot be an algebraic curve since by the Abhyankar-Moh-Suzuki theorem any embedded disk is equivalent to the standard disk. We can add double points to this curve, whilst preserving the Orevkov invariant, to make it seem more like a polynomially parametrised curve. Nevertheless, the link at infinity of this does not arise as the link at infinity of an algebraic affine plane curve. It would be interesting to characterise those links at infinity that do arise from a similar construction of a non-abelian Orevkov invariant.
